findings.title: HA stop mid-solve raises a persistent solve_worker_fallback repair that no later solve ever clears
findings.claim: When EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_STOP fires while a solve's reply is being read from the process worker, the reap breaks the pipe, _await_optimize takes the fallback route (one in-process GIL solve during the stop) and raises the persistent 'solve_worker_fallback' repair; after a restart the issue is still raised once the new instance has solved twice through a healthy worker (count 1, null control 0).
findings.mechanism: _shutdown_process_pool kills the child before taking the lock (by design, D1-s2-05), so the in-flight _run_in_process reads EOF and raises ProcessWorkerUnavailable('Ran out of input'); _await_optimize treats that like a broken install: _note_worker_fallback creates the issue with is_persistent=True and reruns the solve in process. The issue is cleared only by _clear_worker_fallback, which returns early unless THIS process's _WORKER_FALLBACK_CAUSES latched a cause for the entry; after the restart the module dict is empty, so every successful solve leaves the restored issue in place. HA does not unload entries at stop, so _release_registrations' clear does not run either.

findings.title: tests/harness.py lifecycle helpers skip HA's on_unload processing: 1 shutdown per unload (HA 2), 4 leaks per NotReady (HA 0)
findings.claim: The suite's entry-manager instrument diverges from Home Assistant's ConfigEntry in two seams of one mechanism (_async_process_on_unload): ha_unload_entry calls each async_on_unload callback FIFO and drops a returned coroutine, so HeatPumpOptimizerCoordinator.async_shutdown runs once per unload where HA runs it twice (1 RuntimeWarning per unload; store saves 3 vs 4 per unload); and ha_setup_entry runs no unload callback when async_setup_entry raises ConfigEntryNotReady, so each failed attempt leaves 4 live registrations reaching its coordinator and the coordinator alive (3 of 3 after 3 failures), where HA's order leaves 0 and 0.
findings.mechanism: homeassistant ConfigEntry._async_process_on_unload: `while self._on_unload: if job := self._on_unload.pop()(): self.async_create_task(hass, job)` then awaits the tasks; the stub DataUpdateCoordinator registers `config_entry.async_on_unload(self.async_shutdown)` as upstream does; tests/harness.py:ha_unload_entry runs `callback()` and drops the result. Every suite test unloading through it therefore never runs the second HeatPumpOptimizerCoordinator.async_shutdown (pump_arbiter.release -> _persist a second time, legionella release, forget_held) that a real unload runs. On ConfigEntryNotReady HA's ConfigEntry.async_setup also awaits _async_process_on_unload (the coordinator's own _release_registrations and the base-class async_shutdown), which tests/harness.py:ha_setup_entry never runs: production's #236 cleanup is therefore unobservable through the suite's helper, and a test that counts registrations after a NotReady sees leaks HA would not have.

findings.title: A user write landing during a debounced in-flight solve is dropped: plan ignores it until the next interval
findings.claim: When away, economy mode, a manual plan, a comfort-weight reset or a holiday-calendar change is written while a solve started through async_request_refresh (setup's first solve, a button, a service, any state listener) is in flight, the write's re-plan request is dropped by the refresh debouncer and the published plan stays built on the pre-write value until the next scheduled update: 7 of 8 request-refresh census rows stale, 0 of 8 when the in-flight solve came from async_refresh.
findings.mechanism: DataUpdateCoordinator.async_request_refresh goes through Debouncer.async_call, which returns without arming a trailing run while a call is executing (upstream: 'Locked means a call is in progress. Any call is good, so abort.'; the stub mirrors it). The in-flight call is the refresh carrying the solve, so the writer's request never reaches async_run_optimization, whose #1754 re-run latch (_optimization_rerun_requested) only catches calls that arrive there. The scheduled interval refresh bypasses the debouncer, so the same write during a scheduled solve IS re-planned (null control). The stale window is up to one optimization_interval (default 30 min, DEFAULT_OPTIMIZATION_INTERVAL); _mode_superseded covers only the fixed modes.

findings.title: A single-zone install publishes an upper and a lower floor in its space plan
findings.claim: On every single-zone plant (published two_zone_enabled=False) the published space plan carries non-null upper and lower floor temperatures on all 96 forecast rows, so the plan sensor and the card present two floors the configuration does not have; at a clean archive of 92d38ecb this fails 140 of 193 driven d12-cells level cells.
findings.mechanism: OptimizationResult always fills upper_temp_trajectory and lower_temp_trajectory (single zone: both equal the room trajectory), and HeatPumpOptimizerCoordinator._build_plan_views decides two_zone from `bool(result.upper_temp_trajectory and result.lower_temp_trajectory)` rather than from the model's params.two_zone_enabled, so the zone columns are published whenever the lists are non-empty, which is always.

findings.title: Export tree: two_zone_mode 'auto' (the default) turns on a second zone for installs that store no zone key
findings.claim: In the export handed to this seat, every install that stores no zone key and leaves two_zone_mode at its default publishes two_zone_enabled=True and a plan with distinct upper and lower floor trajectories (6 of 6 such plants), while thermal_model.py's own comment and const.py's TWO_ZONE_MODE comment state that 'auto' is the presence rule; a clean git archive of 92d38ecb reads 0 of 6.

findings.title: Scalar Carnot flow-lift factor is inverted: a hotter flow raises COP, and the batch twin disagrees
findings.claim: ThermalModel.flow_lift_factor returns carnot_ref/carnot_flow (>1 above the 35 C reference, 1.586 at a 60 C flow and 0 C outdoor) while _batch_cop multiplies by carnot_flow/carnot_ref (<1), so every scalar COP priced at a flow above the reference (valved buffer, every DHW charge, a direct plant's curve) is boosted instead of derated and simulate_trajectory_batch disagrees with simulate_trajectory on 14 897 trajectory elements over the valved/combi/wood/coil arms. On the 50 published golden plans flow_lift_factor returned >1 on 1268 calls.
findings.mechanism: thermal_model.py:3391 `return max(0.25, carnot_ref / carnot_flow)` against thermal_model.py:4483 `np.maximum(0.25, carnot_flow / carnot_ref)`. compute_cop (valve: flow_temp = tank), compute_cop_dhw (flow = tank water) and the curve-flow lift all route through flow_lift_factor; the batch twin, used for the solver's finite-difference gradient, carries the physical ratio. Consequences: the scalar objective prices hot storage cheaper the hotter it is (DHW COP 2.89 at 35 C, 4.26 at 55 C, 4.58 at 60 C at 0 C outdoor), and the gradient the solver follows is of a different physics than the objective it scores.

findings.title: mixing_valve.emitter_delivery returns negative heat: a cold tank behind the valve cools the zones
findings.claim: mixing_valve.emitter_delivery returns ua*(mix-zone) without its documented max(0, .) floor, so in the scalar two-zone throttled step a tank colder than a zone draws heat back out of the slab/upper floor into the tank, while the batch twin floors it at 0: 3674 two-zone valve trajectory elements differ even with D2-s1-01 corrected. On the 9 valved golden plans the scalar step booked 496 negative deliveries moving 87.52 kWh from the zones back into the tank (valve_storage_small_tank alone 57.3 kWh).
findings.mechanism: mixing_valve.py:138 `return ua * (mix_temp - zone_temp)` under a docstring 'Never negative: a valve can shut, but it cannot cool a house'. _valve_two_zone_delivery uses it for q_rad and q_floor; simulate_trajectory_batch writes np.maximum(0.0, ...) for the same terms. Below the zone temperature the scalar model runs the emitters as a heat pump in reverse, booking zone heat into the tank (balance still closes, so conservation does not see it).
